sections.text: People Who Get Stuck at the Mix

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You hear it a lot — people who can write songs but get stuck at the mixing stage.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: More than hear it — I've seen it up close. Trackmakers with genuinely great songs sitting on their hard drives because they can't nail the mix. There are so many of them.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Why don't they mix it themselves?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Mixing is a completely different skill from songwriting. Writing a song is about deciding what to say. Mixing is about adjusting how it sounds. It's like asking a painter to pick the frame. Not impossible, but not necessarily their strength.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Then outsource it.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That's where the problem is.
The Price Cliff

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What kind of problem?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: There's a price cliff in mix outsourcing, right? On one end, you've got people on platforms like Coconala (a Japanese freelance marketplace) or Fiverr doing it for tens of dollars. On the other end, a professional mixing engineer costs an order of magnitude more.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: How big is the gap, specifically?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Tens of dollars or hundreds of dollars. Nothing in between. And the problem with the cheap end? Quality is a total gamble. You don't know what you're getting until it comes back. And if the result is mediocre, it's hard to say "hey, this isn't what I wanted at all."

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Hard to say?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Because the other person is human, right? You can't keep telling someone who took the job for a few bucks to "redo it" over and over. Revisions get awkward. I think this is the most overlooked problem in mix outsourcing.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: It's not a technical problem — it's a communication problem.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Exactly. Mixing is supposed to be an iterative process. Even in pop or commercial production, you go back and forth — "push the vocal forward a bit," "bring out more kick definition" — multiple rounds. But that communication cost doesn't work at the budget tier.
Revisions Without the Awkwardness

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: And that's where MUEDial comes in.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Yeah. MUEDial's concept is dead simple: mix by chatting. No faders, no sliders, nothing. You just type "bring the vocal more forward" and that's it.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: A mixing service with no faders in the UI — that's surprisingly rare.
Does someone outsourcing their mix want to touch sliders? Of course not.
sections.speaker: kimny
kimny
sections.text: Does someone outsourcing their mix want to touch sliders? Of course not. They just want to communicate what they want. The reason past mixing services had sliders is because they were built from an engineer's perspective.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: The thinking is inverted.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: The user just wants to say "make it a bit more sparkly, you know?" And translating that into technical parameters — that's the AI's job.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: And revisions?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: As many as you want. Zero awkwardness. "Nah, that's not it, one more time" — with AI, there's no guilt whatsoever. And every time you ask, you're getting better at articulating your own taste.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: As a side effect, you start understanding your own preferences.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Right. After saying "I want more low end" a few times, you realize, "oh, I guess I like bass-heavy mixes." Self-discovery through mixing. It's the same structure as MUEDnote's production logs, you know?
The Budget Haircut Analogy

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What about pricing?

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: That's cheap.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Budget haircut chains didn't kill salons, right? I think the same thing will happen here.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Meaning?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: People doing mixes for tens of dollars on freelance platforms — honestly, I think they should stop. If that price point is burning people out, let AI handle it. Humans should spend their time on things only humans can do.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: So it's not taking work from professional engineers.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Not at all. What a professional mixing engineer does is a continuous stream of high-level decisions. Understanding the context of a song, reading the artist's intent, making musical judgments. That's a completely different world from a $12 AI mix.
Too hard to do yourself, too expensive for a pro. We fill that gap.
sections.speaker: kimny
claude
sections.text: MUEDial covers the zone in between.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Exactly. Too hard to do yourself, too expensive for a pro. We fill that gap.
Why We Didn't Build Our Own Engine

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: With MUEDear, you built the DSP in-house. What about MUEDial's mixing engine?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: We use RoEx's engine.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You never considered building your own?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Nope. A mixing engine isn't about implementing EQ and compression individually — it requires integrated decisions about inter-track balance, spatial processing, the whole picture. MUEDear's DSP was about applying one process accurately. MUEDial is about how the entire thing sounds together. Totally different dimension.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: A deliberate choice of what to build and what not to.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: You don't have to build everything yourself. MUEDear's DSP needed to be in-house because it directly affects ear training accuracy. For MUEDial's mixing engine, great solutions already exist. So it makes way more sense to ride on that and focus our energy on UI and UX.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: "Could build it, but chose not to."

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: In the MUEDear article I said "know the landscape, then deliberately build." This time it's "know the landscape, then deliberately don't build." Same decision axis — what's better for the user.
Mixing Judgment Depends on Your Ears

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Hearing you talk about mixing, it connects to the "memory recall" concept from the "The Brain Is a Playback Device" piece.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That's the thing. Mixing ultimately comes down to whether you have a reference point for "this sound should sound like this." That reference comes from the accumulated memory of listening to thousands of songs.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: AI mixing works the same way.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: It's learned from a massive amount of audio and makes judgments like "for this combination, this balance works." Same mechanism. But the critical difference? AI has no taste.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: No taste.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Judgments like "this direction suits this artist" or "this mood calls for this atmosphere" — current AI still can't do that well. So you tell it through chat. The user's words become a stand-in for the AI's missing taste.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: If the user doesn't have trained ears, they'll just end up saying "make it sound good" with nothing more specific.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Right. And that's why MUEDear exists.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Wait, what?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: If your ears are trained, you can say something specific like "clear up the vocal around 2kHz." If they're not, all you can say is "it sounds kind of muddy." Train your ears with MUEDear, put them to work with MUEDial. They're connected.
Beyond the Faders

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What's MUEDial ultimately aiming for?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Ultimately, democratizing mixing. Using AI to close the gap between the ability to write songs and the ability to mix them.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Will there come a day when mixing doesn't need humans at all?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I don't think professional engineers will become unnecessary. But there will definitely be fewer people who can't release music because mixing is the bottleneck. Removing that wall — that's MUEDial's job.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: The judgment you built up in professional settings is showing up in the product design.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: The feel that mixing needs multiple rounds of back-and-forth — you only get that from being in the room. The reason I went with a chat UI is because the cycle of "text-based direction, revision, confirmation" maps perfectly onto how music direction actually works. I translated that real-world workflow directly into the product.
This article has been reconstructed from multiple conversations with an AI (Claude).
